What is irritating to the eyes are chemicals formed when chlorine bonds with nitrogen. Urine, dirt, leaves and grass are all sources. These chemicals still kill germs, but they are irritating. You need to remove them by raising the chlorine level very high. As long as the pH levels are good you can have a high level of chlorine without irritation. When the water is a bit cloudy and smells really "chemical" then you know that these byproducts are high and will be irritating. This concludes my general knowledge on pool chemistry.

This is hardly breaking news guys. Learned all this in a general science class long ago. You normally keep the pool at a low level of chlorine. As the free chlorine bonds with any source of nitrogen it forms byproducts. These byproducts are what you normally associate as smelling like chlorine at a pool, as they start to build up the water is a bit cloudy and smells strongly of chlorine even though the total level is still around normal. This is when it hurts your eyes. To get rid of the byproducts you hyperchlorinate, take the chlorine up to a higher level. This shocks the byproducts out of the pool. The problem is that you need to keep the pH level on the ball when the chlorine is that high or it will be irritating. If you have the pH in the golden zone a higher level of chlorine is not at all irritating. The reason pool managers don't shock the byproducts out of the system all the time is because the pH has probably gone too high to correct. You can drop it down a bit with acid but as calcium is leached out of the pool walls it will eventually set up a buffered solution, forcing the pH more basic and preventing the pH from dropping. At this point you need to dump water and start fresh. So all pool managers know about this, and don't care that the pool is irritating because the chemicals still kill germs. Plus they have learned to hate kids.

That wasn't in the class, but: Shock treatment adds a larger than normal amount of oxidizing chemicals to pool water. This additional dose destroys organic contaminants and oxidizes ammonia and nitrogen compounds to rid the area of irritating odor and, if chlorine is used for the purpose, to sanitize the water.

The software contributed to the issue. With no internal angle of attack indicator and no visibility, the pilots were confused when the stall warnings stopped. In an article in a magazine, a noted journalist noted that once the angle of attack was so extreme, the system rejected the data as invalid and temporarily stopped the stall warnings. However, "this led to a perverse reversal that lasted nearly to the impact: each time the pilot happened to lower the nose, rendering the angle of attack marginally less severe, the stall warning sounded again—a negative reinforcement that may have locked him into his pattern of pitching up" which increased the angle of attack and thus prevented the plane from getting out of its stall

The problem is that in the four minutes after the autopilot disengaged, they apparently never realized that they were stalled because they had no reliable gauge of airspeed. The stall alarm turned off when the nose was raised at an extreme angle because of the impossible instrument readings, and restarted when they lowered the nose. The engines were at 100 load throughout. It looks like the copilot fuxored them keeping the nose up, the captain probably never realized the control was still pulled back as his were not, as the controls are not linked. All they knew was that the altitude indicator was dropping, but since the airspeed indicators were wildly fluctuating and the stall alarm seemed random they probably died very confused. All in all, not a great example of shitty piloting, the software seems to have been crap.

Fly by wire foolishness. It is likely that they didn't realize that the controls would permit them to make inputs that would lead to a stall, as they usually wouldn't. But if the failsafes were in play they autopilot wouldn't have kicked out. I think that the non linked controls, a lack of a telltale that makes sure the pilots know what the mode (law) of the plane is at all times and most importantly a clear visual indicator of angle of attack were the takeaways that the manufacturer had to fix after they finally dug up the black box. Fixing the airspeed pitons so that they didn't fill with ice was the initial problem, they had no reliable airspeed indicators , and this is what knocked them out of autopilot in the first place. The pitons were flagged and were going to be replaced in a major city, tragically. We still don't know what happened exactly. When the captain showed up from his nap, they were pitched 30% and at the service ceiling at 38000 feet.  He put the nose down but this made the stall alert come back on so it is presumed the copilot kept jerking it back to make the stall alarm go away. It is kind of nightmarish to imagine waking up from a nap and sitting down in the pilot seat with a panicked copilot, an intermittent stall alarm, no visuals, airspeed randomly reading as -200, 0 and 200 knotts and as you buckle in the altitude starts to plummet.  The real criticism is that they never did a read of all indicators and controls as a crew, presumably the captain would have figured out that the reason they were in a cant was the copilot's stick and he would have nosed down until their altitude was steady. The engines never quit so I have to imagine that a more experienced pilot would have been able to ignore the stall alarm and storm turbulence to get a feel of when the wings had lift.

Right, we have only seen two or three extended periods where he has both gone deep into counts and also had a hot power streak. I would say early last season, which seemed more like a pitch zone selection thing that pitchers started working around, and mid way thru the previous decade, which ended towards the end of the season as he started to lunge again. This whole walking AND home run thing is a new player as far as I can tell. My personal theory, and it is pulled out of my ass, is that the manager put him at #1 in the lineup and then did a manager jitsu that went like this... We don't have a number one hitter. This team needs YOU to lead this team. He was able to lead this team when we needed him to, if we want to get to the world series we NEED you to lead us there. Because the player wants to win. He was already the leader of this team in every way that counted, but at some level his personal at bats reflected a bit of the kid going for glory. The only selfish thing about the player as a player has been his desire for the big mash. At some deep level he is a little kid that wants that glorious feeling of mashing a low fastball on the sweet spot of the bat, and it is indeed a glorious feeling, one of the most magical in sports, when you make that contact where the bat and the ball and your arms turn into a crazy yo-yo that launches the ball farther than seems possible. He wants it more than a big contract. He wants it more than the hall of fame. But I think putting him in the one spot has finally clicked that magic switch, the little kid wants to meet his responsibility as team leader more than he wants to be a hero, to mash that ball. And as we all knew, as he had to know at every level except the most important one deep in his brain muscle memory, by going deep into the count he still will get that chance to mash the ball, even if he lays off what could be a low fastball, but really is a slider headed for the plate. So the manager dumped an unfair load on his shoulders and he found his shoulders stronger than he thought. Or, he is doing a zone hitting thing that pitchers figure out mid July and fucks him over till late August. Either way I love that kid, I am just hoping for the one that puts him in Cooperstown, because the statue at the local stadium either has him blowing a bubble or I am putting it on myself.
